q: According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, the emf induced in a coil is proportional to the:
o: Rate of change of magnetic flux linking the coil
Current already flowing in the coil
x: Faraday's law: emf = −N ΔΦ/Δt, so the emf depends on how fast the flux changes, not on the size of the flux itself. A large but steady flux induces no emf.

q: The flux through each turn of a 100-turn coil falls from 0.05 Wb to 0.01 Wb in 0.2 s. The average emf induced in the coil is:
x: emf = N ΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 0.04 / 0.2 = 20 V. Leaving out N gives 0.2 V, and leaving out the time gives 4 V.

q: A bar magnet is held at rest inside a coil connected to a galvanometer. The galvanometer shows:
o: A steady deflection, because flux links the coil
A deflection that grows with time
No deflection, because the flux through the coil is not changing
A deflection only if the magnet is very strong
x: An emf is induced only while the flux linking the coil changes. A stationary magnet gives a constant flux, so no emf and no current, however strong the magnet.

q: A magnet is pushed into a coil, and then pushed in again over the same distance at twice the speed. The induced emf the second time is:
x: The same change in flux now happens in half the time, so ΔΦ/Δt doubles and the induced emf doubles.

q: A rate of change of magnetic flux of 1 weber per second is equivalent to:
x: From emf = ΔΦ/Δt, the unit of induced emf is Wb s⁻¹, which equals the volt.

q: A coil of 50 turns, each of area 0.02 m², lies at right angles to a magnetic field that rises uniformly from 0 to 0.5 T in 0.1 s. The emf induced in the coil is:
x: ΔΦ per turn = ΔB × A = 0.5 × 0.02 = 0.01 Wb, so emf = 50 × 0.01 / 0.1 = 5 V. Leaving out N gives 0.1 V and leaving out the area gives 250 V.

q: A flat coil lies in a uniform, steady magnetic field. Which action will NOT induce an emf in the coil?
o: Rotating the coil about one of its diameters
Increasing the strength of the field
Sliding the coil sideways within the uniform field without turning it
Squeezing the coil so that its area becomes smaller
x: Sliding the coil within a uniform field keeps B, A and the angle the same, so the flux does not change and no emf is induced. The other actions change the flux.

q: A 200-turn coil of area 0.05 m² is in a uniform field of 0.1 T. It is turned in 0.5 s from having its plane perpendicular to the field to having its plane parallel to the field. The average induced emf is:
x: Flux per turn falls from BA = 0.1 × 0.05 = 0.005 Wb to zero. emf = NΔΦ/Δt = 200 × 0.005 / 0.5 = 2 V; leaving out N gives 0.01 V.

q: The magnetic flux through a coil increases uniformly with time. The emf induced in the coil:
x: A uniform increase means ΔΦ/Δt is constant (the Φ–t graph is a straight line with a fixed slope), so the induced emf is constant.

q: A straight rod 0.5 m long moves at 4 m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform field of 0.2 T, with the rod, its velocity and the field all mutually perpendicular. The emf across the rod is:
x: The rod sweeps area at a rate Lv, so emf = BLv = 0.2 × 0.5 × 4 = 0.4 V.

q: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is such that it:
o: Aids the change in flux that produces it
Opposes the change in flux that produces it
Is always along the magnetic field
x: Lenz's law: the induced current sets up a magnetic effect that opposes the change causing it. This is the meaning of the minus sign in emf = −N ΔΦ/Δt.

q: Lenz's law is a direct consequence of the law of conservation of:
x: Because the induced current opposes the change, work must be done against it, and that work becomes the electrical energy produced. Energy is not created from nothing.

q: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards one end of a closed coil. The end of the coil facing the magnet becomes:
o: A south pole, attracting the magnet
A north pole, attracting the magnet
A north pole, repelling the magnet
Unmagnetised, because the coil is not iron
x: To oppose the approaching north pole, the induced current makes the near face a north pole, which repels the magnet.

q: The north pole of a bar magnet is pulled away from one end of a closed coil. The end of the coil facing the magnet becomes:
o: A north pole, repelling the magnet
A south pole, repelling the magnet
A north pole, attracting the magnet
A south pole, attracting the magnet
x: The induced current opposes the withdrawal, so the near face becomes a south pole that attracts the retreating north pole.

q: Suppose the current induced in a coil helped a magnet to move towards it instead of opposing it. This would:
o: Create electrical energy without any work being done, breaking energy conservation
Reduce the emf to exactly half
x: An induced current that helped the motion would speed the magnet up, which would make more current, and so on, producing energy from nothing. That is why the induced current must oppose the change.

q: A bar magnet is dropped through a horizontal copper ring that has a narrow cut across it. Ignoring air resistance, the acceleration of the magnet as it approaches the ring is:
x: An emf is induced, but the cut means no closed circuit, so no current flows and there is no opposing force. With a complete ring, an induced current would oppose the fall and the acceleration would be less than g.

q: The north pole of a magnet is moved towards the face of a flat coil. Viewed from the side of the magnet, the induced current in the coil flows:
o: In no direction, as no current is induced
x: The near face must become a north pole to oppose the approach, and a face behaves as a north pole when current seen from that side is anticlockwise.

q: Which statement about Faraday's law and Lenz's law is correct?
o: Faraday's law gives the size of the induced emf and Lenz's law gives its direction
Lenz's law gives the size of the induced emf and Faraday's law gives its direction
Both laws give only the direction of the induced current
Lenz's law applies only to steady magnetic fields
x: Faraday's law gives the magnitude, N ΔΦ/Δt, and Lenz's law, through the minus sign, gives the direction of the induced emf and current.

q: Two coils P and Q share the same axis. The current in P flows clockwise, as seen from one end, and is increasing. Seen from the same end, the induced current in Q flows:
x: P's increasing flux through Q is opposed by an induced current in the opposite sense, so Q's current is anticlockwise. If P's current were decreasing, Q's current would be clockwise.

q: A metal rod is pulled at steady speed along two conducting rails in a uniform magnetic field, forming a closed circuit. The magnetic force on the induced current in the rod:
o: Opposes the motion of the rod, so work must be done to keep it moving
Acts in the direction of motion and speeds the rod up
Is zero because the rod moves at steady speed
Acts along the length of the rod
x: By Lenz's law, the force on the induced current opposes the motion. The pulling agent does work against this force, and that work appears as electrical energy in the circuit.

q: A transformer works on the principle of:
x: A changing current in the primary coil produces a changing flux in the core, which induces an emf in the secondary coil. Induction between two coils is mutual induction.

q: A transformer does not work with a steady direct current in its primary coil because:
o: A steady current produces a constant flux, so no emf is induced in the secondary
Direct current cannot flow through copper coils
The iron core blocks direct current
Direct current makes the flux reverse too rapidly
x: Induction needs a changing flux. A steady DC gives a constant flux in the core, so after switch-on no emf is induced in the secondary.

q: The iron core of a transformer is made of thin insulated sheets (laminations) in order to:
o: Reduce the energy lost through eddy currents in the core
Increase the number of turns on the secondary coil
Allow current to flow from the primary coil to the secondary coil
Make the core a permanent magnet
x: Laminations break up the paths of eddy currents induced in the core, so less energy is wasted as heat. No current passes through the core from one coil to the other.

q: The core of a transformer is made of soft iron mainly because soft iron:
o: Conducts electricity well, so current passes from the primary to the secondary
Is a permanent magnet that supplies the magnetic flux
Has such a high resistivity that it never needs laminating
Is easily magnetised and demagnetised, so it links the flux of both coils with little hysteresis loss
x: Soft iron concentrates the changing flux so that it links both coils, and it loses little energy each time it is magnetised and demagnetised. It still needs laminating to reduce eddy currents.

q: An ideal transformer has 500 turns on its primary and 100 turns on its secondary. If the primary is connected to 220 V AC, the secondary voltage is:
x: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = 220 × 100/500 = 44 V. Using the ratio upside down gives 1100 V.

q: A transformer steps 240 V AC down to 12 V. Its primary has 1000 turns. The number of turns on its secondary is:
x: Ns = Np × Vs/Vp = 1000 × 12/240 = 50 turns. Inverting the ratio gives 20000, and 20 is the turns ratio itself.

q: An ideal transformer changes 220 V AC to 11 V AC and supplies a current of 2 A from its secondary. The current in the primary is:
x: For an ideal transformer, power in = power out: Vp Ip = Vs Is, so Ip = 11 × 2 / 220 = 0.1 A. Multiplying by the turns ratio the wrong way gives 40 A.

q: An ideal transformer with a turns ratio Ns : Np = 4 : 1 is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. The output of the secondary is:
x: The voltage is multiplied by Ns/Np = 4, giving 880 V. A transformer changes the voltage but not the frequency, which stays 50 Hz.

q: The low-voltage, high-current winding of a transformer is made of thick copper wire. This mainly reduces:
o: Eddy current losses in the core
x: Thick wire has low resistance, so the I²R heating (copper loss) caused by the large current is reduced. Eddy current and hysteresis losses happen in the core, not the windings.

q: An ideal transformer has 200 primary turns and 800 secondary turns. The primary is connected to 50 V AC and the secondary to a 100 Ω resistor. The primary current is:
x: Vs = 50 × 800/200 = 200 V, so Is = 200/100 = 2 A. Power in = power out gives Ip = 200 × 2 / 50 = 8 A.

q: At a power station, the voltage of the generated electricity is raised before it is sent along transmission lines. This is done with:
x: A step-up transformer raises the voltage, and so lowers the current, for long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers are used near consumers.

q: Electrical power is sent over long distances at very high voltage because:
o: High voltage makes the resistance of the cables zero
For the same power, the current is smaller, so less energy is lost as heat in the cables
High voltage increases the current, so more power reaches homes
High voltage changes AC into DC, which travels farther
x: P = VI, so a higher V means a smaller I for the same power, and the heat loss I²R in the cables falls sharply. The cable resistance itself does not change.

q: The power lost as heat in a transmission line of resistance R carrying current I is given by:
o: V²/R, where V is the transmission voltage
I²R, where I is the current in the line
VI, where V is the transmission voltage
IR, where I is the current in the line
x: Heat loss in the cable is I²R. V²/R with the full transmission voltage is wrong because that voltage is not across the cable; VI is the total power sent, and IR is the voltage drop in the cable, not a power.

q: The same power is transmitted through the same cables, but the transmission voltage is raised 10 times. The power lost as heat in the cables becomes:
x: Ten times the voltage means one-tenth the current for the same power. Loss = I²R, so it falls by a factor of 10² = 100.

q: In an ideal step-up transformer, compared with the primary coil, the secondary coil has:
o: More turns, a higher voltage and a larger current
Fewer turns, a higher voltage and a smaller current
More turns, a higher voltage and a smaller current
Fewer turns, a lower voltage and a larger current
x: Step-up means Ns > Np, so Vs > Vp. Since power in = power out, the secondary current must be smaller.

q: Near homes, the high voltage of transmission lines is reduced to the mains value of about 220 V by:
x: Step-down transformers at local substations and on poles lower the voltage to a safe value for household use.

q: In a step-down transformer, the secondary winding usually has:
x: Step-down needs Ns < Np. The secondary carries the larger current, so it is wound with thicker wire to keep its I²R heating low.

q: A power of 2 MW is transmitted at 200 kV through lines of total resistance 10 Ω. The power lost as heat in the lines is:
x: I = P/V = 2 × 10⁶ / 2 × 10⁵ = 10 A, so the loss is I²R = 100 × 10 = 1000 W = 1 kW, only 0.05% of the power sent.

q: The same power is to be sent along a transmission line. Which change would NOT reduce the energy lost as heat in the line?
o: Using a metal of lower resistivity for the cables
x: Lowering the voltage raises the current for the same power, which increases the I²R loss. The other changes reduce either the resistance or the current.
